'''David Eugene Smith''' (January 21, 1860 – July 29, 1944) was an [[Americans|American]] mathematician, educator, and editor.

==Education and career==
David Eugene Smith is considered one of the founders of the field of mathematics education. Smith was born in Cortland, New York, to Abram P. Smith, attorney and surrogate judge, and Mary Elizabeth Bronson, who taught her young son Latin and Greek.<ref>{{cite journal|last=DONOGHUE|first=EILEEN F.|title=In Search of Mathematical Treasures: David Eugene Smith and George Arthur Plimpton|journal=Historia Mathematica|year=1998|volume=25|issue=4|pages=359–365|doi=10.1006/hmat.1998.2203|doi-access=free}}</ref> He attended [[Syracuse University]], graduating in 1881 (Ph. D., 1887; LL.D., 1905).  He studied to be a lawyer concentrating in arts and humanities, but accepted an instructorship in mathematics at the Cortland Normal School in 1884 <ref name="maa">{{Cite web | url=http://www.maa.org/history/presidents/smith.html | title=David Eugene Smith, 1920 MAA President &#124; Mathematical Association of America}}</ref> where he attended as a young man. While at the Cortland Normal School Smith became a member of the Young Men's Debating Club<ref>An Honorable Record: Some of the alumni of the Young Men's Debating Club. Cortland Evening Standard, Friday, April 12, 1895.</ref> (today the [[Delphic Fraternity]].) He became a professor at the [[Michigan State Normal College]] in 1891 (later Eastern Michigan University), the principal at the [[State University of New York at Brockport|State Normal School]] in [[Brockport, New York]] (1898), and a professor of mathematics at [[Teachers College, Columbia University]] (1901) where he remained until his retirement in 1922<ref>{{Cite book |title=A history of school mathematics |date=2003 |publisher=National Council of Teachers of Mathematics |isbn=978-0-87353-471-0 |editor-last=Stanic |editor-first=George M. A. |location=Reston, VA |pages=1644 |chapter=Chapter 36: The U.S. Mathematics Education Research Community |editor-last2=Kilpatrick |editor-first2=Jeremy}}</ref>.  

Smith became president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] in 1920<ref name="maa" /><ref>{{cite journal|title=Religio Mathematici. Presidential address delivered before the Mathematical Association of America, September 7, 1921|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=28|issue=10|date=October 1921|pages=339–349|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044102896305;view=1up;seq=379|doi=10.2307/2972153|jstor=2972153|last1=Smith|first1=David Eugene|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and served as the president of the [[History of Science Society]] in 1927.<ref>The History of Science Society [http://www.hssonline.org/about/society_presidents.html "The Society: Past Presidents of the History of Science Society"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212134009/http://www.hssonline.org/about/society_presidents.html |date=December 12, 2013 }}, accessed 4 December 2013</ref> He also wrote a large number of publications of various types. He was editor of the ''Bulletin'' of the [[American Mathematical Society]]; contributed to other mathematical journals; published a series of textbooks; translated [[Felix Klein]]'s ''Famous Problems of Geometry'', Fink's ''History of Mathematics'', and the [[Treviso Arithmetic]]. He edited<ref>[[G. B. Mathews]] (1916) [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v97/n2421/pdf/097077a0.pdf A Budget of Paradoxes] From [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] 97:77 to 79 (#2421)</ref> [[Augustus De Morgan]]'s ''[[A Budget of Paradoxes]]'' (1915) and edited <ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1932-05393-9|title=Book Review: ''A Source Book in Mathematics'' edited by David Eugene Smith |year=1932 |last1=Karpinski |first1=L. C. |author-link=Louis Charles Karpinski|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=38 |issue=5 |pages=333–335 |doi-access=free }}</ref> ''A Source Book in Mathematics'' (1929). He wrote many books on Mathematics which are listed below.
He served as Mathematics Editor of the 14th edition of the [[Encyclopedia Britannica]], 1929.  ''Abacus'' and ''Algebra'' were his own contributions to the first volume.

== Revival ==
In 2020, [[Francis Su]] published ''Mathematics for Human Flourishing'', in which he cites Smith's speech entitled "Religio Mathematici" (Latin: faith of a mathematician), his farewell address delivered to the [[Mathematical Association of America]] in 1921.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Su |first=Francis Edward |title=Mathematics for human flourishing |date=2020 |others=With Christopher Jackson |isbn=978-0-300-23713-9 | publisher=Yale University Press|location=New Haven |oclc=1090441053}}</ref>

An annotated collection of Smith's writings was published in 2022. It includes postcards (digitized by the Cortland Historical Society), poetry, speeches, and various excerpts from his works. In the foreword, [[Francis Su]] writes of Smith: "He rekindled the awe I experienced when I first saw the beauty and depth of mathematics, an awe that I—as a mathematician who now takes these things for granted—might have long since forgotten."<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=David Eugene |title=In the Shadow of the Palms: The Selected Works of David Eugene Smith |publisher=Science Venerable Press |others=Foreword by Francis Su |year=2022 |isbn=978-1-959976-00-4 |editor-last=Abbey |editor-first=Tristan |location=Alexandria, Va |pages=xi |language=English |author-link=David Eugene Smith}}</ref>
